analysis.one_liner: Forces fast-track votes on legislation to cut federal funding for Medicare's prescription drug benefit whenever spending exceeds set targets.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee: it got no hearing, no vote, and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have the Secretary of Health and Human Services check every year whether federal general revenue spending on Medicare's Part D prescription drug benefit exceeds set dollar targets, from $25.7 billion in 2006 up to $73.1 billion in 2013. If it did, a 'funding warning' would be declared, and the President would have to send Congress a plan to eliminate the excess funding within 15 days of submitting his budget. The bill then sets special fast-track procedures: the plan must be introduced within 3 days, committees must act by June 30, and if they don't, the bill can be pulled out of committee onto the floor with limited debate and sharply restricted amendments. The goal is to make it hard for Congress to simply ignore a required cut to the drug benefit's funding.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers concerned about the long-term federal deficit, and high-income households in particular, since general revenue taxes fund the drug benefit and capping that spending reduces pressure for future tax increases. It also serves deficit-focused policymakers who wanted a mechanism to force consideration of entitlement cuts that would otherwise die in committee.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the HHS Secretary to determine each year whether general revenue funding for Part D exceeds specific target amounts, treating an affirmative finding as a Medicare Part D funding warning.
Requires the President, within 15 days of submitting his budget, to send Congress proposed legislation responding to any such funding warning.

Creates expedited House and Senate procedures — mandatory introduction, committee deadlines, discharge motions needing only one-fifth of the House, and limited debate and amendments — so the proposal cannot simply sit and die in committee.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare beneficiaries. If the warning fired, the required legislation would be aimed at eliminating general revenue funding for the drug benefit, meaning benefit reductions or cost shifts to seniors would be on the table — moved on a fast track with little room for opponents to slow it down.

drawbacks.text: The bill does nothing about the underlying cost of the benefit — it targets only general revenue funding, not drug prices or payments to private plans — so the required fix would fall on beneficiaries rather than on what the government pays drugmakers and insurers.
The fast-track procedures waive normal points of order and limit debate to a few hours, making it easier to pass benefit-cutting legislation quickly and harder for opponents to stop it.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the trigger alone cuts nothing: Congress would still have to pass the required legislation, and any year's warning could be avoided if Congress enacted legislation eliminating the excess funding through other means.

The good-faith objection: the drug benefit was brand new, created by the 2003 Medicare law, and the target amounts — $25.7 billion for fiscal 2006 rising to $73.1 billion for 2013 — could have triggered a forced cut proposal almost immediately, putting a benefit seniors had just gotten at risk.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The fiscal-discipline benefit is real but modest and uncertain: the mechanism only forces a presidential proposal and a floor process, not an actual cut. The cost side is concrete and targeted: the trigger is aimed squarely at a newly created senior benefit, and the fast-track rules are designed to make cutting it easier than stopping the cut. For beneficiaries, the downside risk outweighs the fiscal upside.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Lindsey Graham introduced the bill in the Senate on March 9, 2005, joined by Jeff Sessions.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day — its only action in the entire Congress.
The Finance Committee never reported the bill, and it received no floor vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare beneficiaries are better off: the automatic trigger and fast-track path that could have forced benefit-cut legislation never became law. Deficit-focused sponsors lost their mechanism.

for.name: Sen. Lindsey Graham
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Chuck Grassley)
against.role: Committee of referral — held the bill
against.what_they_did: Took no action: the bill sat in committee for the rest of the Congress without a hearing, markup, or vote, and was never reported.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Republicans and the bill never reached a vote, so no recorded opposition or partisan split exists in the record.

industries.industry: Private insurers selling Part D drug plans
industries.note: Part D is delivered through private drug plans, and forced legislation to cut general revenue funding would pressure the plans and their revenue. Their interest in stopping this bill ran alongside beneficiaries' interest in keeping the benefit.

The new drug benefit drives large prescription drug purchases; legislation eliminating excess general revenue funding would shrink that demand. The industry's interest in the bill's failure aligned with seniors'.

The drug benefit is funded from general revenue, which draws on broad income taxes that fall most heavily on higher earners. Capping that spending shifts the risk onto beneficiaries rather than taxpayers.
